q: In Faraday's law written as ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, the negative sign expresses:
o: That the induced emf is always a negative number
The conservation of charge in the coil
Lenz's law: the induced emf opposes the change in flux that causes it
That the flux through the coil always decreases
x: The minus sign shows the direction of the induced emf: it acts to oppose the change of flux, which is Lenz's law. The size of the emf is NΔΦ/Δt; it is not always negative.

q: A straight conductor of length L moves at speed v along the direction of its own length through a uniform magnetic field B that is at right angles to the conductor. The emf induced between its ends is:
x: Moving along its own length, the conductor cuts no field lines: the magnetic force on its charges (along v × B) is at right angles to the rod, so no charge is pushed along it and no emf appears. BLv needs L, v and B mutually perpendicular.

q: The flux through each turn of a 10-turn coil rises steadily from 0 to 0.06 Wb in 0.2 s and then stays at 0.06 Wb. The induced emf during the first 0.2 s and after it is, respectively:
x: While the flux changes, ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 10 × 0.06/0.2 = 3 V; once the flux is constant, ε = 0. Forgetting the 10 turns gives 0.3 V; thinking a large steady flux still induces an emf gives 3 V then 3 V.

q: An aircraft with a wingspan of 20 m flies horizontally at 250 m s⁻¹ where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. The emf induced between its wing tips is:
x: The horizontal wings cut the vertical field component: ε = BLv = 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 20 × 250 = 0.2 V. A slip in the power of ten gives 2 V or 0.02 V.

q: A closed coil of 100 turns, each of area 0.01 m², and total resistance 2 Ω lies at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The field decreases steadily at 0.4 T s⁻¹. The induced current is:
x: ε = NA(ΔB/Δt) = 100 × 0.01 × 0.4 = 0.4 V, and I = ε/R = 0.4/2 = 0.2 A. 0.4 A takes the emf as the current; leaving out N gives 2 × 10⁻³ A.

q: A strong magnet dropped down a vertical copper tube falls much more slowly than an unmagnetised piece of iron of the same size. The reason is that:
o: Eddy currents induced in the tube produce a magnetic field that opposes the magnet's motion
Copper is strongly magnetic and attracts the magnet to its walls
Air resistance is larger for a magnet than for iron
The tube becomes a permanent magnet that repels the magnet
x: The falling magnet changes the flux through each ring of the tube, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law their field opposes the motion that causes them, giving an upward drag. Copper itself is not attracted by a magnet.

q: A flat wire loop lies in the plane of the page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The field strength is increasing. Viewed from the front of the page, the induced current in the loop is:
o: Zero, because the field is uniform
x: The inward flux is increasing, so by Lenz's law the induced current makes a field out of the page, inside the loop. By the right-hand grip rule that needs an anticlockwise current. Clockwise would add to the increasing inward flux.

q: A coil gives an average induced emf ε when the flux through each of its turns changes by ΔΦ in time t. A second coil with twice as many turns has the same change of flux per turn in time t/2. Its average induced emf is:
x: ε = NΔΦ/Δt, so doubling N doubles the emf and halving the time doubles it again: 2 × 2 = 4ε. Counting only one of the two changes gives 2ε.

q: A 50-turn coil of area 0.04 m² lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. It is turned over through 180° in 0.1 s. The average emf induced in it is:
x: The flux per turn goes from +BA = +0.02 Wb to −0.02 Wb, a change of 0.04 Wb. So ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 50 × 0.04/0.1 = 20 V. Taking the change as just BA (as for a 90° turn) gives 10 V; seeing the same magnitude at the start and end gives zero.

q: The self-inductance of a coil, in henry, is numerically equal to the emf induced in it when the current through it changes at the rate of:
x: ε = L(ΔI/Δt), so L = ε when ΔI/Δt = 1 A s⁻¹. A steady current of 1 A induces no emf at all.

q: A soft-iron core is pushed into an air-cored coil. The self-inductance of the coil becomes:
x: Iron greatly increases the flux linked with the coil for the same current, so L = NΦ/I increases strongly. The turns and dimensions are unchanged, but the core material matters.

q: A current changing at 5 A s⁻¹ in coil P induces an emf of 2 V in a nearby coil Q. If instead the current in Q changes at 5 A s⁻¹, with the coils in the same positions, the emf induced in P is:
x: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the same either way: M = 2/5 = 0.4 H. So the same rate of change in Q induces 0.4 × 5 = 2 V in P. 0.4 is the value of M in henry, not the emf.

q: An inductor of 0.25 H stores 2 J of energy in its magnetic field. The current through it is:
x: U = ½LI², so I² = 2U/L = 4/0.25 = 16 and I = 4 A. Forgetting the square root gives 16 A; dropping the ½ gives I² = 8, about 2.8 A.

q: When a switch in a circuit containing a large inductor is opened, a spark often jumps across the switch contacts. This is because:
o: The inductor's resistance suddenly becomes very large
Opening the switch increases the current in the inductor
The current falls very quickly, inducing a large emf in the inductor
The battery's emf rises when the circuit is broken
x: Breaking the circuit makes ΔI/Δt very large, so the self-induced emf L(ΔI/Δt) is large enough to ionise the air across the gap. The induced emf tries to keep the current flowing, but the current itself does not increase.

q: The wire of a standard resistance coil is doubled back on itself before it is wound, so that the current goes one way along one half and back along the other half. This is done so that:
o: The magnetic fields of the two halves cancel and the coil has almost no self-inductance
The resistance of the coil is halved
The coil stores more magnetic energy
The coil has a very large self-inductance
x: In a doubled-back (non-inductive) winding the two halves carry equal, opposite currents side by side, so their fields cancel and almost no flux links the coil; its inductance is negligible while its resistance is unchanged.

q: For an inductor, the energy stored (vertical axis) is plotted against the square of the current, I² (horizontal axis). The graph is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 0.25 J A⁻². The self-inductance is:
x: U = ½L × I², so the gradient is ½L = 0.25 J A⁻², giving L = 0.5 H. Taking the gradient as L itself gives 0.25 H.

q: Two air-cored solenoids have the same number of turns per metre and the same cross-sectional area, but solenoid Y is twice as long as solenoid X. The ratio of their self-inductances, L(Y) : L(X), is:
x: L = μ₀N²A/l. Y has twice the length and so twice the turns: L(Y)/L(X) = (2²/2) = 2. Equivalently L = μ₀n²Al with n fixed, so L ∝ l. Squaring the turns without dividing by the doubled length gives 4 : 1.

q: When the current in a coil changes by 2 A in 0.1 s, an emf of 20 V is induced in it. The energy stored in the coil when it carries a steady current of 3 A is:
x: L = ε/(ΔI/Δt) = 20/(2/0.1) = 1 H, and U = ½LI² = ½ × 1 × 9 = 4.5 J. Dropping the ½ gives 9 J; forgetting to square the current gives 1.5 J.

q: In a simple DC generator, the output current is made to flow in one direction in the external circuit by:
x: The split rings reverse the coil's connections to the brushes every half turn, just when the coil's emf reverses, so the external current keeps one direction. Slip rings give an AC output.

q: For an ideal transformer, which quantity is the same for the primary and the secondary?
x: An ideal transformer has no losses, so VpIp = VsIs: the power in equals the power out. Voltage and current change in opposite ratios set by the turns ratio.

q: In a simple AC generator, the coil rotates steadily in a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf is zero at the instant when the plane of the coil is:
o: Parallel to the field, where the flux linking it is zero
Perpendicular to the field, where the flux linking it is greatest
Never: the emf is never zero
x: ε = NABω sin ωt, with ωt measured from the position where the plane is perpendicular to B. There the flux is greatest but momentarily not changing, so the emf is zero. The emf is greatest when the plane is parallel to the field.

q: The coil of an AC generator is made to rotate twice as fast in the same field. The peak emf and the frequency of the output, respectively:
x: ε₀ = NABω, so doubling ω doubles the peak emf, and f = ω/2π also doubles. Speed changes both, not just the frequency.

q: The back emf in the armature of a DC motor, running on a fixed supply, is greatest when the motor:
o: Runs at its highest speed with no mechanical load
Has just been switched on from rest
Is heavily loaded and slows down
x: The back emf is the generator emf of the rotating armature, so it is proportional to the speed. It is largest at the highest speed (no load) and zero when the armature is at rest.

q: A power of 100 kW is sent along a transmission line of total resistance 5 Ω at a voltage of 10 kV. The power lost as heat in the line is:
x: The line current is I = P/V = 100 000/10 000 = 10 A, so the loss is I²R = 100 × 5 = 500 W. At 1 kV the current would be 100 A and the loss 50 kW, which is why high voltages are used.

q: The output of a simple DC generator with a single coil and a split-ring commutator is:
o: Perfectly steady, like that of a battery
Zero on average over a complete turn
In one direction, but rising from zero to a maximum and back twice every turn
x: The commutator only reverses the connections; the coil's emf still varies as sin ωt, so the output is the rectified shape |sin ωt|: one direction but pulsating, with two peaks per revolution.

q: An AC generator has a peak emf of 200 V. Its coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. At the instant the plane of the coil makes an angle of 60° with the field direction, the instantaneous emf is (sin 60° ≈ 0.87, cos 60° = 0.5):
x: The emf is greatest when the plane is parallel to the field and zero when it is perpendicular, so ε = ε₀ cos(angle between plane and field) = 200 × cos 60° = 100 V. (Equivalently, the normal is at 30° to B and ε = ε₀ sin 30°.) Using sin 60° gives 174 V.

q: A DC motor with armature resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 220 V supply and draws 20 A at its working speed. The mechanical power developed in the armature is:
x: Back emf ε = V − IR = 220 − 20 = 200 V, and mechanical power = εI = 200 × 20 = 4000 W. Check: input VI = 4400 W minus heat I²R = 400 W gives 4000 W. 4.4 kW is the input power.
